en: The Sūtra on the Lazy Farmer Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Huìjiǎn.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
He was accompanied by a multitude of twelve hundred and fifty people as well as a host of bodhisattvas.

At that time, the Buddha intended to travel from Rājagṛha to Śrāvastī. The bodhisattvas led the way, dressed in the garments of Śakra and Brahmā—and their bodies appeared like those of the Four Heavenly Kings—while the community of bhikṣus followed behind the Buddha. The devas, nāgas, and spirits made offerings from above.

Not far from the city, there was at that time a man plowing a field. From afar he saw the Tathāgata’s disciples and their attendants, who were upright and exceptionally wonderful, with majestic and towering spiritual power; their countenances were as beautiful as the moon among the stars, endowed with marvelous marks and manifold excellences, radiating a serene golden light, and possessing all thirty-two major signs that manifested every excellence.
Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, his heart was filled with joy; he wished to approach the Buddha, prostrate himself in worship, and inquire about the meaning of the Dharma.
"A Buddha appears in the world but rarely; such an occasion occurs only once in a long while."
Withdrawing, he thought to himself, "The plowing is not yet finished and the sowing is not yet complete; I shall see the Buddha only at a later leisurely time.

At that moment, the World-Honored One, knowing that his mind had given rise to such indolence, smiled and emitted five-colored rays of light. The light issued from his mouth and illuminated the realms of the ten directions, bringing peace and security to the five paths of existence. All beings, riding upon the light, gathered at the place where the Buddha was: those in the hells found rest, the hungry ghosts were satiated, the animals conceived thoughts of goodness, the people sought deliverance, and the devas, nāgas, and spirits listened to the Dharma.

The wise Ānanda, having understood the seven factors—meaning, dharma, time, occasion, and his own person as well as that of others—went to where the Buddha was, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason do you smile?"
"Since he has laughed, there must certainly be some meaning behind it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you see that plowman?"
He replied, "I have seen them.
The Buddha said:

"From the time of Vipaśyin Buddha until now, for ninety-one kalpas, this person has been farming here; yet whenever he encounters a Buddha, he is always indolent and chooses what is soft and easy. Furthermore, he later busily farms the unwholesome dharmas of birth and death, failing to recognize the plow of the Dharma or how to sow in the field of the infinite."

Having passed through six Buddhas without receiving deliverance, you now see me; yet as soon as you give rise to a wholesome thought, you immediately change your mind and regret it, wishing to remain indolent and delighting in planting the roots of sin.
Hearing this from afar, the people abandoned their plowing and fields and came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, repenting and reproaching themselves:
“We were foolish and ignorant; our transgressions are most grave. We pray that you will take pity on us and forgive these offenses.”
"Shrouded in darkness and confusion, we have long been obstinate and indolent; may you grant us your forgiveness and deliver us from birth and death.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
"If you are able to awaken, it will be of benefit to you regarding the Dharma; it shall never cause you harm.
The Buddha preached the sutra for him, demonstrating the defilement of indolence and the benefits of diligence. [The youth] leaped with joy and established himself in non-retrogression.
Countless thousands of devas, nāgas, and spirits all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
"For this reason, those who study the Way must always be diligent; do not be indolent, lest you wander through birth and death for many kalpas."
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the venerable Ānanda, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and asura kings rejoiced upon hearing the sutra; they paid homage and withdrew.
The Sūtra on the Lazy Plowman Spoken by the Buddha
